caption:
नितेश तिवारी की मच-अवेटेड फिल्म Ramayana से जुड़ी एक बहुत ही चटपटी खबर सामने आई है! 🎬

फिल्म में भरत का रोल प्ले कर रहे एक्टर आदिनाथ कोठारे ने Hindustan Times को दिए इंटरव्यू में कई मजेदार बातें शेयर की हैं। आदिनाथ ने खुलासा किया कि उन्होंने शुरुआत में लक्ष्मण के किरदार के लिए ऑडिशन दिया था, जो रोल बाद में Ravie Dubey को मिला। 🎭

ऑडिशन में उन्हें सीता माता को कुटिया के अंदर रहने की हिदायत देने वाला सीन करना था। लगभग 6 महीने लंबे प्रोसेस के बाद उन्हें भरत के रोल के लिए सेलेक्ट किया गया। आदिनाथ का मानना है कि बड़े और अनुभवी एक्टर्स को भी ऑडिशन देने से कभी पीछे नहीं हटना चाहिए। 💡

इंटरव्यू में उन्होंने Ranbir Kapoor के साथ अपने बचपन के कनेक्शन का भी ज़िक्र किया। आदिनाथ ने बताया कि मुंबई के Bombay Scottish School में 7th क्लास के दौरान उनके कॉमन फ्रेंड Binoy Gandhi ने उन्हें Ranbir Kapoor से मिलवाया था। 🏫

वैसे, क्या आपको भी लगता है कि बॉलीवुड के बड़े स्टार्स के लिए ऑडिशन देना जरूरी होना चाहिए? अपनी राय कमेंट्स में जरूर शेयर करें! 👇

ctx.title: Addinath Kothare met Ranbir Kapoor in school, recalls auditioning for Lakshman before landing Bharat's role in Nitesh Tiwari's Ramayana | Interview
ctx.summary: Addinath Kothare talks to Hindustan Times about playing Bharat in Nitesh Tiwari's Ramayana, working with Ranbir Kapoor, and more.
ctx.text:
Actor Addinath Kothare has steadily made his mark across Marathi and Hindi cinema. In 2019, his directorial Paani, in which he also played the lead role, won the National Film Award for Best Film on Environment Conservation. He has since continued to explore different projects, including Kabir Khan's 83, several web series and the recently released Nayyi Naveli. The actor is now seen as Bharat in Nitesh Tiwari's Ramayana , also known internationally as Ramayana: Rise of a Legend. In a conversation with Hindustan Times, Addinath talks about initially auditioning for Lakshman before being cast as Bharat, working with Ranbir Kapoor, filming the emotional Bharat Milap sequence and why he considers the filmmaker's screenplay a masterclass.
Landing the role of Bharat was not an overnight process. The actor went through several rounds of auditions over several months before being finalised for the part. He also opens up about working with Nitesh Tiwari and Ranbir, and the experience of shooting one of the film's most emotional moments, the Bharat Milap sequence.
Addinath and Ranbir have an interesting connection that goes back to their school days. Both actors studied at Mumbai's Bombay Scottish School, and the actor still has a faint memory of seeing Ranbir on the school premises when he was in the seventh standard.
He shares how a common friend, Binoy Gandhi, who lived in his building and is now a filmmaker, introduced him to Ranbir. “I remember seeing Ranbir in school. I had a common friend who used to stay in my building. He is also a filmmaker today; his name is Binoy Gandhi. He had introduced me to Ranbir once in school. I have a very vague memory of this tall, thin person sitting on the railing of the senior building. I was probably in the seventh standard,” he recalls. Addinath also reveals that he may have brought up the school memory during a later conversation with Ranbir. Interestingly, he believes the actor also remembered the incident.
Addinath reveals that his association with Ramayana began with an audition for the role of Lakshman, which eventually went to Ravie Dubey. The casting process, led by Mukesh Chhabra, required him to perform a scene in which Lakshman asks Sita to stay inside the kuti (forest hut) before drawing the rekha (line), requesting her to not step out for safety reasons. Looking back, the actor believes the audition was also about finding actors who could convincingly look like a family on screen. “I tested for the scene where Lakshman tells Sita to stay in the kuti. That was probably a benchmark test to find the family of Shri Rama because we all had to look like we belonged to the same family,” he recalls.
It was nearly six months after the audition that Addinath received a call informing him that he had been shortlisted. The experience also reinforced his belief that auditions are not just for newcomers and that established actors should be equally open to the process. He feels there is a misconception that actors with experience should not have to audition. “There is a completely wrong notion that people have about auditions. Nobody comes to theatres just to see faces. They come if they like the story. Today, there is so much talent around us. Even if there are 10 good actors, it does not necessarily mean all of them will get the right opportunities,” he says.
Talking about why he continues to audition despite having years of experience, Addinath points out that casting is about finding the actor who fits a particular character best. He adds, “There are so many actors who can play a particular part. How will the director decide who is right for it? Today's casting directors are experimenting and giving opportunities to new and fresh faces. As actors, we need to help filmmakers push their boundaries. Auditions are very crucial. Internationally, even A-list actors audition.”
